There Is No Such Thing As An Ordinary Day

There is a particular light that happens at around 4 p.m. on a Tuesday in October. It is not the dramatic golden light of summer sunsets or the thin, austere light of deep winter. It is a practical, honest light. It comes in sideways through windows that haven't been washed since spring and lays itself across kitchen counters, office desks, and bus seats without any pretense. For most of our lives, we are taught to wait for the extraordinary light — the sunrise over the mountain, the fireworks, the moment on stage — and to tolerate everything else as filler. But I have come to believe that the 4 p.m. Tuesday light is where nearly everything important actually happens.

I want to write about that light. Not because it is spectacular, but precisely because it isn't.

We live in a culture that is obsessed with beginnings and endings. We love origin stories and finales. We love the first day of school, the first kiss, the first line of a novel, the grand opening, the product launch. We love the graduation, the wedding, the final chapter, the reveal, the denouement. What we are much worse at is talking about the middle. The middle is where you have already started but are nowhere near finished. The middle is where motivation has worn off but habit has not yet taken hold. The middle is maintenance, repetition, tending, and care. And because we don't have good stories for the middle, we mistakenly think that nothing is happening there.

But the middle is where life lives.

### 1. The Myth of Arrival

When I was younger, I believed in arrivals. I believed that life was a series of thresholds and that if I could just cross the next one, I would finally feel settled. If I got into the right school, I would feel smart. If I got the right job, I would feel secure. If I found the right person, I would feel loved. If I published something, moved somewhere, achieved something, I would finally arrive at the version of myself I was supposed to be.

What no one told me is that arrival is a feeling that lasts for about three days. Psychologists have a name for it — the arrival fallacy — the assumption that happiness awaits us at the next milestone. Tal Ben-Shahar coined the term, but every human being has lived it. You get the thing you wanted so badly and you feel ecstatic, then relieved, then normal again. The hedonic treadmill hums along. The brain, brilliant and ungrateful as it is, recalibrates.

This is not a tragedy. It is actually a kind of mercy. If we stayed in the ecstasy of arrival forever, we would never get anything else done. But it does mean we have been telling ourselves the wrong story. We think life is a mountain we climb to reach a summit where we can finally rest. In reality, life is more like walking. The point was never to get to the end of the walk. The point was walking.

For years I kept a notebook where I wrote down all the things I thought would fix me. It was an embarrassing and earnest list: learn to speak French fluently, run a half-marathon, have an apartment with a balcony and plants that don't die, be the kind of person who answers emails promptly. One by one, I did some of those things. I did not become fluent in French, but I can order coffee and have a halting, joyful conversation about books. I ran the half-marathon and spent the next week limping down stairs. I got the balcony. The plants still died sometimes. And none of it fixed me, because I was never broken. I was just in the middle.

Once you stop waiting to arrive, a strange freedom opens up. You can start paying attention to what is actually here.

### 2. Attention as a Form of Love

The writer Mary Oliver famously said, "Attention is the beginning of devotion." I would go further: attention *is* devotion. What we attend to, grows. What we ignore, withers, not because it was unworthy but because we never watered it.

We talk a lot about love as a grand emotion, a lightning strike, a fate. But love, in practice, is mostly attention. It is noticing that your friend always tugs at their sleeve when they are anxious. It is remembering how your partner takes their coffee. It is listening to a child tell the same long, winding story about a dream they had with dinosaurs and teachers and not checking your phone while they do it.

Attention is not passive. It is an active, muscular act. In an economy that monetizes your distraction, choosing to pay attention is almost a rebellion.

I have been trying to practice a very small form of this rebellion for the last few years. I call it the "one beautiful thing" practice. Every day, wherever I am, I try to find one beautiful thing that I would have otherwise missed. Not a beautiful sunset — those are too easy, they demand to be seen — but a small, shy beauty. The way the steam from a pot of rice makes a perfect circle on the underside of a cabinet. The chipped blue paint on a doorway that reveals five other colors underneath it, like geological strata. The way an old man on the subway folded his newspaper with absolute precision, even though no one was watching.

At first it felt forced, like homework. After a few weeks, something shifted. My brain, which had been trained to scan for problems and threats and to-do lists, began to scan for beauty without being asked. It is not that the world became more beautiful. It is that I finally adjusted my eyes to see what had been there all along.

There is a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi*, which finds beauty in imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. A cracked bowl mended with gold, a weathered fence, a garden that is intentionally a little wild. Wabi-sabi is not about lowering your standards; it is about raising your sensitivity. It asks you to love things not despite their flaws but because the flaws are proof that they have lived.

People are like that too.

If you practice attention long enough, you start to realize that you have never actually seen the place where you live. You have seen your idea of it, your commute through it, your errands within it. But you have not really looked. Try walking a street you walk every day and pretending you have been hired to photograph it for someone who has never been there and never will be. Suddenly you notice the second-floor balcony with all the potted cacti, the hand-painted sign for a tailor that has been there since 1987, the tree that has grown around a chain-link fence and absorbed it. The world is dense with detail if you give it time.

### 3. The Smallest Museums

I love museums, but I have come to love small, unofficial museums even more. Not the Louvre or the Smithsonian, but the museums that people make without meaning to.

The junk drawer in a kitchen is a museum. It holds the history of a household in miniature: dead batteries, takeout menus for restaurants that have closed, a single key no one can identify, birthday candles, rubber bands, a tiny screwdriver from assembling furniture three moves ago. No curator arranged it, and yet it tells a perfect, honest story.

A bookshelf is a museum. Not the curated, color-coded kind you see on the internet, but the real kind. The paperback with the cracked spine that someone has read four times, the hardcover that was a gift and has never been opened but is kept out of guilt and affection, the odd souvenir guidebook from a trip taken years ago. If you want to know a person, look at the books they keep and the books they pretend they will read again.

A pocket is a museum for a day. Receipts, a hair tie, a smooth stone picked up on a walk because it fit perfectly in the palm, loose change.

We are all archivists. We are all leaving trails. Long after we are gone, the most telling artifacts of our lives will not be the grand statements but the small, accumulated evidence of how we actually spent our days. Did we keep letters? Did we save voicemails? Did we fold our laundry with care or throw it on a chair? These are not trivial questions. They are the texture of a life.

One of my favorite places in any city is the hardware store. It is a museum of solutions. Every aisle is a taxonomy of human problems and the patient, clever ways we have invented to solve them. Little bags of washers and anchors and brackets, each designed for one specific, unglamorous job. Someone, somewhere, had a wobbly chair or a leaking pipe or a door that wouldn't latch, and someone else thought, *I can make a piece of metal that fixes that*. There is something deeply optimistic about a hardware store. It believes the world can be repaired.

We need more reverence for repair. We celebrate innovation, disruption, the new. But repair is a quieter, more radical act. To repair something is to say: this still matters. You are not disposable. I will take the time to understand you and make you whole again. That applies to chairs and to people.

### 4. How Tools Shape Thought

We like to think we use tools, but tools also use us. They shape the way we think.

The clock taught us that time is linear, divisible, and scarce. Before mechanical clocks, time was cyclical and task-based — you planted when it was planting time, you ate when you were hungry. After clocks, time became something you could waste, save, spend, and lose. Language followed. Our relationship to mortality changed.

The map taught us that the world is something you can see from above, abstracted into lines and borders. A map is incredibly useful, but it also lies. It makes a living landscape look fixed and knowable. It was only when I started navigating by landmarks instead of by GPS that I realized how differently I experienced a city. With GPS, I was a blue dot being pulled along a line. Without it, I had to remember: turn left at the bakery that smells like butter, go straight until the mural of the woman with the yellow flowers. I was not above the city; I was inside it.

Now we live inside the tools of the internet, and they are shaping us in ways we are only beginning to understand. The feed teaches us that information should be infinite, fast, and personalized. The search bar teaches us that every question has an answer and that the answer should arrive in 0.4 seconds. The like button teaches us that every thought can be measured.

These tools are not bad. They are extraordinary. I can video call my grandmother who lives three thousand miles away. I can learn how to fix a faucet at 2 a.m. from a stranger in New Zealand. I have access to more poetry, music, and art than any human in history could have consumed in ten lifetimes. But every tool has a bias, and the bias of the feed is that what is recent is most important, and what is loudest is most true.

The antidote is not to throw the tools away. It is to use them consciously, and to keep older tools alive as well. Handwriting is a tool. Walking without headphones is a tool. A long conversation without an agenda is a tool. Boredom is a tool — one of the most powerful ones we have, because it is in boredom that the mind finally wanders somewhere unprompted.

I worry sometimes that we are losing our tolerance for being unfinished. Everything online wants to be polished, captioned, concluded. But real thinking is messy and provisional. Real learning requires saying, "I don't know yet." We need places — in our lives and in our minds — where things are allowed to be drafts.

### 5. On Being a Good Ancestor

There is a question that has been haunting me in a good way. It comes from Jonas Salk, who asked, "Are we being good ancestors?"

It is a strange question because we are so trained to think of ourselves as descendants. We think about our parents and grandparents, the heritage we received. We rarely think about the heritage we are leaving. But we are, every single day, making a world that someone else will inherit.

Being a good ancestor does not require you to do something huge. It does not mean you have to start a foundation or write a great book. It can mean planting a tree whose shade you will never sit in. It can mean writing down a recipe exactly as your mother made it, with the note that says "add a pinch more salt if it is raining." It can mean cleaning up a trail, voting, volunteering to read to kids, maintaining a friendship for thirty years.

There is a story about a man in Japan, Hiroshi Kuroda, who spent decades planting trees on a mountain that had been deforested. People thought he was eccentric. He planted and tended, slowly, one by one. That forest now holds the soil, cleans the air, shelters birds. His grandchildren play there. He will not be remembered on any global list, but the mountain remembers him.

On a smaller scale, I think about the digital ancestors we are becoming. Every photo we post, every comment we leave, every piece of data we generate is a fossil for the future. What will future historians conclude about us from our feeds? That we were anxious, performative, hilarious, kind? That we cared a lot about what we ate for lunch? The archive is being built whether we curate it or not.

I have started to think of my own life as a letter to someone I will never meet. Not a grand letter, but a practical one. *Here is what I learned about making soup when you are sick. Here is how I apologized when I was wrong and why it was hard. Here is the book that made me understand my father better.* If someone found that letter a hundred years from now, would it be useful? Would it be kind?

The future is not an abstraction. It is a place where someone will live, and it is being made out of our present choices about attention, repair, and care.

### 6. The Permission to Be Ordinary

Perhaps the most liberating idea I have ever encountered is that you are allowed to have an ordinary life and still have it be meaningful.

We have been sold a story that a meaningful life must be a remarkable life — that you must be exceptional, visible, celebrated. Social media amplifies this to an almost unbearable degree. Everyone seems to be building a brand, launching something, traveling somewhere incredible. The algorithm rewards extremes.

But most lives, by definition, are not extreme. Most lives are lived in apartments and houses, on commutes, in grocery stores, in conversations around small tables. And if we believe that only extraordinary lives matter, we will spend our one precious life feeling like we are failing.

An ordinary life can still be an astonishing one. You can still learn to make the perfect omelet, not because it will make you famous but because it is a small mastery that brings delight. You can still be a steadfast friend, a careful neighbor, a person who knows the names of the birds in your neighborhood. You can still keep a journal that no one will ever publish but that makes your thoughts clearer to yourself.

I think about my grandmother, who never left the state where she was born. She kept a garden that was almost absurdly productive — tomatoes, cucumbers, zinnias that grew taller than I was as a child. She did not do it for recognition. She did it because she liked putting her hands in dirt and because she liked giving people bags of tomatoes that were still warm from the sun. Was her life ordinary? By the world's metrics, yes. Was it meaningful? Utterly. I still dream about those tomatoes.

We need a better definition of success. One that includes: Did you love well? Did you notice things? Were you good company for yourself on a rainy afternoon? Did you leave things a little better than you found them?

If you can answer yes to even two of those, you have done magnificently.

### Coda

It is now 4:15 p.m. The light has moved. It is no longer on the counter; it is on the floor now, making a long, thin rectangle that my cat has decided is exactly where she needs to sleep. Outside, someone is wheeling a trash bin down the sidewalk, and it makes that clattering sound that is unmistakable and oddly comforting. A bus sighs to a stop.

Nothing extraordinary is happening. And everything is.

If you have read this far, thank you. I have no grand conclusion to offer, no five-step plan, no final revelation. Only an invitation, if you want it: Look up from whatever screen or page you are on, and find one small, shy beauty where you are. The way light hits a wall, the sound of water in pipes, the particular green of the plant by your window. Let it be enough for a moment.

We spend so much of our lives waiting for the big moments to give us permission to feel alive. But aliveness is not waiting on the other side of a threshold. It is here, in the middle, on a Tuesday, at 4 p.m., in whatever room you happen to be in.

You have not missed it. You are in it.
